paragraphs.text: There were three children: Gerald, Jimmy, and Kathleen. And they were at school in a little town in England. The boys were at one school, of course, and their sister was at another.

They used to see each other only on weekends. So they looked forward to going home for summer vacation. But one year they couldn't go home because someone in the family had the measles. That disease was easy to catch.
After many letters back and forth, their parents agreed to let them stay at Kathleen's school. All the girls had gone home. All the teachers had left except the French teacher.
Now the boys had arrived, and they were drinking tea with Kathleen.
"We need a summer project," she said. "Let's write a book."
"Too much work," said Gerald, who was the oldest. "We'll do something outdoors. A cave would be good. We could eat our meals there."
"There aren't any caves," said Jimmy, who liked to say no. "And I doubt Mademoiselle will let us go out by ourselves."
"Well, I'm going to talk to her," said Gerald.
He washed his hands and combed his hair before he knocked on Mademoiselle's door. She was reading.
"Excuse me, Mademoiselle," said Gerald politely. "I thought I'd say hello because you're in charge of us."
Mademoiselle was charmed by the young man's manners. "Can I do anything for you?"
"No, thank you. We don't want to be any trouble. In fact, we would cause less trouble tomorrow if we spent all day outside."
Mademoiselle smiled. "I know what you really want. You want to be left alone."
Gerald laughed and Mademoiselle did too.
"Go ahead," she said. "I won't stand in your way."
The next morning the children went off on their adventure. It was a beautiful day.
"We're sure to find something ," said Gerald. "A boy at school said that there was a cave near here. But he said there's an enchanted castle too. So none of that may be true."
The children walked along the road, which was very hot. They decided to share a drink from their lunch.
Soon they came to a fork in the road. They went right and came to another fork and then another.
"We're completely lost," said Kathleen. "What fun!"
Now the trees arched overhead and bushes lined the banks along the road.
"Let's have some lunch," said Jimmy.
As they sat down, Gerald leaned against some bushes. "Oh my!" he cried.
The bushes gave way and he almost fell backward. The other two pulled back the bushes. There was a large hole in the bank.
"It's a cave!" said Gerald. "I'm going in."
"Oh, don't!" said Kathleen. "There might be snakes."
But Gerald was already crawling through the hole.
"It is a cave! Come look!"
Kathleen and Jimmy followed him down the hole. They walked a short distance and came out into the sunshine.
"How wonderful!" said Kathleen. Ahead of them was a tall arch framed with ferns and grasses.
"It looks like a train tunnel," said Jimmy.
"It's the entrance to the enchanted castle," said Kathleen.
"Oh, don't be silly." Gerald led the way to the arch.
"There's a set of steps!" said Jimmy.

They followed Gerald down the steps, walking slowly through the darkness. Up ahead was a patch of daylight. The children passed under another arch and out onto a terrace. Below them was a lake with an island. Beyond that, marble statues gleamed among the trees. White towers stood out against the sky.
"It's the enchanted castle!" cried Kathleen.

Gerald and Kathleen were certain that the white towers belonged to an enchanted castle. Jimmy was not so sure. They walked through a beautiful garden until they came to a maze. They tried to find the center of the maze. But it was impossible!
"What's that?" Gerald picked up a red thread on the ground. One end was tied to a thimble, but the other end . . .
"There is no other end!" Gerald realized. "Maybe it leads to something!"
"I think the gardener put it there," said Jimmy.
"Look at the crown on that thimble," said Kathleen. "Do you think a gardener would have a princess' silver thimble?"
"Let's follow the thread." Gerald walked forward, winding the thread around his fingers as he went. The thread led them into the middle of the maze.

There they found a circle of green lawn with a sundial in the center. All around the edge of the circle was a marble seat. The thread ran across the lawn. It ended in the hand of someone sleeping on the seat!
"It's an enchanted princess!" said Gerald.
"Her clothes are so old-fashioned," said Kathleen. "She must have fallen asleep a hundred years ago."
"She isn't really a princess," said Jimmy.
Gerald and Kathleen laughed. They didn't care what Jimmy said. Every part of the adventure—the cave, the maze, the thread—felt magical to them.
"Lift up the veil, Gerald," whispered Kathleen. "If she's beautiful, we'll know she's a princess."
"Lift it yourself," he said.
Kathleen gently lifted the veil. "Isn't she lovely?"
"Not too bad," Gerald muttered.
"Now, Gerald, you must wake the princess," said Kathleen.
"She's not a princess," insisted Jimmy. "She's only a little girl dressed up like a princess. Look at how long her dress is. She won't be any taller than Gerald when she stands up."
Kathleen ignored him. "Gerald, you're the oldest. You have to kiss her awake."
"Not me!" cried Gerald. "She'll slap me the minute she wakes up."
"Then I'll do it," said Kathleen. "But I don't think it'll do any good." And it didn't.
"I don't mind kissing her," said Jimmy. "I'm not afraid like some people."
With that, Jimmy planted a loud kiss on the princess' cheek. The three children stood waiting to see what would happen next.
The princess opened her large, dark eyes. She stretched her arms and yawned. Then she said, "So the hundred years are over? Which one of you is my hero?"
"I am," said Jimmy.
"My prince." The princess held out her hand and Jimmy shook it hard.
"But you aren't really a princess, are you?" he asked.
"Of course I am. Look at my crown." She pulled aside her veil to reveal a crown of diamonds. "How did you ever get past the dragons?"
Gerald ignored her question. "Then this really is an enchanted castle?"
"Of course it is. Don't be stupid." The princess stood up and her dress fell in waves around her feet.
"I told you her dress would be too long," said Jimmy.
"It must have grown over the years," said the princess. "Let's go back to the castle, and I'll show you all my lovely jewels. Would you like that?"
"Yes," said Gerald. "But . . ."
"But what?" The princess sounded impatient.
"But we're awfully hungry. We never got to eat our lunch."
The princess looked at the sundial. It was three o'clock. "You've had nothing to eat for hours. But think of me. I've had nothing to eat for a hundred years!"

The children walked in a slow parade toward the castle. They were sure that they had stepped into a fairy tale. At last they arrived in a large hall filled with wooden benches and tables. Suits of armor and old flags stood against the walls.
"Wait here," said the princess. "And don't talk while I'm gone. This castle is full of magic. I don't know what will happen if you talk."
Jimmy wanted to say that he didn't think anything would happen. But he didn't.

The princess returned, carrying a tray. "I could only find bread and cheese and water, but it doesn't matter. They'll turn into anything you like—unless you have some dreadful secret fault. What would you like to eat?"
"Roast chicken," said Kathleen. She watched as the princess cut some bread and laid it on a plate.
"Green peas?" The princess cut a piece of cheese and laid it beside the bread. Then she handed the plate to Kathleen. The boys asked for roast beef and cabbage.
Kathleen cut the bread as if she was eating roast chicken. But it still looked and tasted like bread. She wondered what her secret fault was as she watched the boys eat their food.
"This is a game, isn't it?" said Jimmy. "Pretending we're eating roast beef."
"But it is beef. Look at it." The princess opened her eyes very wide.
"Of course," said Jimmy weakly. "I was just joking."
Everyone was very hungry. They ate and drank and felt much better.
"Now if you're finished," said the princess, "I'll show you my treasures."
They followed her down a long hall to some steps. Underneath the steps was a door hidden by a tapestry.
"This door leads to my private apartments," said the princess.

She guided them through a dark corridor until they came to a room. The princess went in first and threw open the shutters. The small domed room was filled with light. Its blue ceiling was painted with gold stars. But the room was empty.
"Where are the treasures?" Kathleen asked politely.
"Don't you see them?" said the princess.
"No," said Jimmy. "And don't try fooling us again. There's nothing here."
"Then I guess I'll have to say the charm," said the princess. "Close your eyes, please."
The princess chanted some nonsense words. There was a creaking, rustling sound.
"Open your eyes now."
The children could not believe their eyes. Silver dishes, gold cups, and diamond crowns lined shelves around the room. All around were piles of necklaces, rings, and bracelets.
"Oh my!" Gerald whispered.
"Now do you believe I can do magic?" asked the princess.
"Yes!" said Kathleen. "May we touch?"
"Go ahead."
The children had great fun playing with the treasures. Suddenly Kathleen had a thought. "Do your parents know you're awake?"
"Oh . . . uh . . . yes," said the princess. "I told them when I got the bread and cheese. They're busy right now. Here, try this bracelet."
"What's this old stuff over here?" asked Jimmy.
"Those are all magic things!" said the princess.
"What does this ring do?" asked Gerald.
"It makes you invisible."
"I'd like to try that," said Jimmy.
"No, I'm the only one who can touch these things. If anyone else tries, they'll lose their magic. Close your eyes and I'll demonstrate the ring."
The children closed their eyes.
"Now count to fifty."
Gerald counted aloud. Everyone could hear a creaking, rustling sound. ". . . 49, 50."
The children opened their eyes. The jewels had vanished, and so had the princess.
Luckily the princess had also told the children how to make her reappear. "If we close our eyes," said Gerald, "she'll reappear when we count to fifty. One, two, three, four . . ."
Gerald and Kathleen closed their eyes, but Jimmy kept his open. Soon he saw a panel under the window slowly open.
"I knew it was a trick," he thought before he closed his eyes.
At fifty the children opened their eyes. But there was still no princess.
"I think there's a secret cupboard under the window," said Jimmy. "Maybe she's hiding in it."
"You looked! That's cheating!" said the voice of the princess. The voice was so close to Jimmy's ear that he jumped. But the princess was still invisible.
"Where is she?" cried all three children at once.
"Should we close our eyes and count again?" asked Kathleen.
"Don't be silly!" The princess sounded angry.
"We're not silly," said Jimmy. "We know you're hiding."
"You think you're so clever pretending not to see me." The princess sounded hurt. "All right, I'll play your game."
"But we can't see you," said Gerald.
"Really?" The princess sounded afraid now.
"We told you that," said Jimmy. He suddenly leaned backward and forward. Then it happened again.
"What's wrong?" asked Kathleen.
"She shook me!"
"And I'll shake him again if he says he can't see me."
"What are you so grumpy about?" Gerald was quite calm. "You said you'd be invisible and you are."
"I'm not. You're just pretending not to see me."
"On my word of honor, you're still invisible," said Gerald.
There was silence. Then the princess said, "Come, I'll let you out. I'm tired of playing with you."
They followed her voice out of the treasure room. She led them through some other rooms. One room was lined with mirrors.
Gerald suddenly said to the princess, "Give me your hand." He pulled her in front of a mirror. "Now look for yourself."
"Oh!" cried the princess in despair. "I am invisible. What shall I do?"
"Take the ring off," said Kathleen.
"It won't come off! But it can't be the ring. Rings don't make you invisible."
"You said this one did," said Kathleen.
"I was only playing at magic. I just hid in the secret cupboard."
"But you can do magic," said Gerald. "What about the jewels?"
"That's only a secret button that makes the panels open. What shall I do?" The princess was crying.
Kathleen moved toward the voice and wrapped her arms around the invisible princess. "I'll tell the king and queen."
"But they were only a game like . . ."
"The bread and cheese," Jimmy said triumphantly.
"And the story I told you in the maze. I wasn't really asleep for a hundred years." The princess sniffed.
"But if you're not the princess, who are you?" said Kathleen.
"My aunt works here. She'll be angry if she finds you. Run outside to the Temple of Flora. I'll meet you there after I close up the treasure room."
The three children went to the Temple of Flora. It was cool and restful inside.
Soon they heard footsteps and saw a shadow on the ground.
"The door to the treasure room has blown shut," said the princess. "It's locked and the key's inside!"
"Sit down and we'll talk about what to do," said Gerald. "But first tell us your name."
"My . . . my name is Mabel Prowse." The princess' voice was broken with sobs. "And . . . and I'm the housekeeper's niece at the castle!"
"I knew she wasn't really a princess," said Jimmy. The others were silent.
"Can we do anything for you, Mabel?" Gerald asked kindly. "If not, we should be going."
"Yes, I want my tea," said Jimmy.
"Tea?" Mabel snapped. "You'd leave me after getting me into this mess?"
"That's unfair!" Gerald began. "We—"
"Leave Mabel alone," interrupted Kathleen. "It must be horrid to be invisible."
"It is. And it's horrid to have an aunt who doesn't like me. She wouldn't let me go to the fair today because I disobeyed her."
"You'll have to tell her about the ring," said Kathleen.
"No! Take me with you."
"I suppose you could come home for tea," said Gerald. "Then we'll decide what to do."
The children agreed that Mabel should leave her aunt a note. Gerald took out his notebook and pencil. They watched the pencil move by itself as Mabel wrote:
Dear Aunt,
You won't see me again for a while. A rich lady in an automobile adopted me. We are going away on a ship. Don't try to follow me.
Mabel
"But that's all lies," said Jimmy.
"If I said I was invisible, she'd think that was a lie too."
By the time they arrived home, they were very late for tea.
"Are you all right?" asked Mademoiselle. "I was worried."
"We're sorry," said Gerald.
"Come in," said Mademoiselle. "You'll have supper now."
There were only three plates at the table, so Jimmy let Mabel have his. He shared with Kathleen. It was strange to see Mabel's food floating in the air and then disappearing.
Everyone was hungry. The cook grumbled when she had to bring more food.
"It'll be hard to give Mabel breakfast," said Gerald. "Mademoiselle will be here then."
"We'll have to buy things and feed her in secret," said Kathleen.
"Our money won't last long," said Jimmy. "Mabel, do you have any money?"
"No," said Mabel, "but I've got lots of ideas."
That night Kathleen lent Mabel one of her nightgowns. As Mabel pulled off her princess clothes, they became visible. As she put on the nightgown, it disappeared. She and Kathleen soon fell asleep.
The next morning Kathleen woke to find Eliza, the maid, staring at Mabel's princess clothes. They were piled on a chair.
"Where on earth did you get those?" asked Eliza.
"Oh . . . oh . . . someone lent them to me for a play we're doing," said Kathleen. She was saved from saying more by the doorbell. Eliza hurried away to answer it.
Mabel got up and began to wash her invisible face in the basin.
"I wish you hadn't written such lies to your aunt," said Kathleen.
"What's the use of telling the truth if no one believes you?"
"You should always tell the truth. Now I'm going to breakfast. Stay quiet up here, and I'll bring you something to eat."
When Eliza came to make the bed, Mabel untucked the corners of the sheets.
"Drat these sheets!" Eliza exclaimed.
Then Eliza swept the floor.
"Don't forget to sweep under the rugs!" Mabel whispered in her ear.
Eliza turned white and ran from the room.
Meanwhile Kathleen and Gerald had decided they must tell Mabel's aunt the truth. So after Mabel's breakfast, the children started walking to the castle.
"Mabel, get behind me," said Kathleen. "Then our two shadows will look like one."
But as they walked through town, a woman noticed a large, black shape on Kathleen's back.
"Hey, missy!" the woman shouted. "What have you been leaning against?"
Everyone walked a little faster.
The children arrived at the castle and found Mabel's aunt reading a romance novel.
"Excuse me," said Gerald, "I believe you've lost your niece."
"I didn't lose Mabel. She left."
"Did you get her note?" asked Kathleen.
"Yes, and I'm happy she's living with a rich lady."
Jimmy couldn't be quiet a moment longer. He had to tell Mabel's aunt the truth. "Mabel's invisible! She's standing right beside me."
"Don't lie to me!" The aunt glared at Jimmy. "Please remove this boy. I'm quite happy about Mabel."
" Well! " said Gerald. He was puzzled by this aunt who didn't care about her missing niece. "But what will Mabel's parents say?"
"Mabel's parents are dead," the aunt said calmly.
The children talked to Mabel's aunt for a few more minutes. She gave them permission to wander over the castle grounds. But she still didn't seem concerned about Mabel.
"Good-bye, children," she said and went back to reading.
When the children were outside again, Mabel said, "I knew she'd believe my note. She reads lots of romance novels. Strange things always happen in her books."
Mabel suggested they walk to the Temple of Flora. When they were seated, she said, "I'm hungry, and you can't keep stealing food for me. I'll have to pretend to be a ghost in the castle."
"You must stay with us until you can remove the ring," Kathleen said kindly.
"I think we need to earn some money for food," said Mabel. "Let's go to the fair. Gerald can do magic tricks for money."
"But I don't know any tricks!" said Gerald.
"Don't worry," said Mabel. "I'm invisible. I can make it look like you're doing tricks."

The fair was about half a mile away. Soon they could hear music from the carousel. Kathleen and Jimmy blended into the crowd while Gerald and Mabel stood in front of a tent. "Ladies and gentlemen," called out Gerald. "My invisible assistant can make money disappear."
A crowd began to gather, and Kathleen and Jimmy joined in. Gerald laid nine pennies on the ground. Mabel picked them up and put them in her pocket to make them disappear.
The audience clapped.
"If you want to see more magic, I'll need to see more money," said Gerald.
The audience dropped more coins onto the ground. Then Mabel made more things vanish. Other things appeared to move around by themselves.
"For my final trick, I will vanish!" said Gerald.
He stepped back, and Mabel wrapped her shawl around him. But nothing happened.
"He can't do it!" someone yelled.
The crowd pushed forward in anger.
"I wish I could put you in my pocket," Mabel whispered to Gerald. "Then you'd be invisible." She squeezed her hands together. "Hey! The ring is loose!"
"Come on!" shouted a man in the crowd. "We paid for a show."
Gerald whispered to Mabel, "Go into the tent. Slip the ring under the canvas to me. When I see you in the crowd, I'll make myself disappear and catch up with you."
Mabel did just that. "I'm back," she said to a surprised Kathleen and Jimmy. "Gerald's wearing the ring. Let's get out of here."
As the children walked away, they heard Gerald announce, "Now I will vanish." Then the crowd roared, and the children knew he had really disappeared this time.
After a few minutes, they heard footsteps on the road but saw no one.
"Hello, I'm over here," said Gerald.
"Good," said Mabel. "I want my ring back."
"Well, you can't have it," Gerald answered. "Because I can't get it off!"
"I wish I were invisible," said Jimmy. The children were walking along in the growing darkness. "I'd be a burglar."
"It's wrong to steal!" cried Kathleen and Mabel together.
"Then I'd be a detective," said Jimmy.
"That's what I'll do," said Gerald, who really was invisible. "Let's go to the police station and see if they need help."
Outside the police station was a notice board. Two dogs had been lost. So had a purse. Gerald wasn't interested in any of that.
Another notice announced that a mansion had been burglarized. Some silver candlesticks and serving dishes were stolen.
"I'll catch those burglars!" Gerald decided. "There's Officer Johnson. Go ask him what he knows about the crime."
The visible children talked to the policeman, but he didn't have much to say.
"Officer Johnson thinks he knows who did it. But he needs proof," Jimmy reported back to Gerald.
"You're not much help," Gerald replied. "You didn't even find out how or when the silver was taken. Go home and eat your supper."
"What will you do about supper?" Mabel asked Gerald as they started walking again.
"I'm hoping one of you will buy me some buns."
The children stopped outside the bakery, and Kathleen and Jimmy went inside.
"Oh!" Mabel suddenly cried.
"What's wrong?" asked Gerald.

"I just remembered I left the window open in the treasure room. I have to go back right now. My aunt will be so angry! The treasure room door is locked from the inside. She'll have to ask the gardener to get a ladder and climb through the window."
"Don't worry," Gerald said. "I can climb through the window." They turned around while Jimmy and Kathleen continued home for supper.
"Late again!" exclaimed Mademoiselle when the two of them arrived. "And where is Gerald?"
"Uh . . . he has a headache," said Jimmy. "He went straight to bed."
"Poor boy. I'll bring him some supper," said Mademoiselle.
"No, no," said Kathleen quickly. "He never eats when he has a headache."
"Oh well," said Mademoiselle. "Hurry up and eat your supper." And she went back to reading some old letters.
Meanwhile Gerald and Mabel arrived at the castle. Mabel knocked on the door the servants used.
"Oh Mabel!" cried her aunt as she opened the door. "Thank goodness you're safe!" She gave Mabel a big hug.

"I don't know what was wrong with me," said the aunt. "Yesterday I didn't care anything about you. The same thing happened when I got your note and when some children visited. But this afternoon I suddenly awoke from my trance and realized you were gone. It was awful!"
Mabel's aunt pulled her into the castle and shut the door.
"That was very strange," said Gerald, who was left outside in the dark. "It seems like more magic to me."
Gerald began looking for the open window of the treasure room. The castle gardens were so beautiful that he felt he was in another world.
"Everything looks so different at night," he thought.

Something white moved under a willow tree. The creature had a goat's horns and legs, but the head and arms of a boy. It stretched its legs, rolled on the grass, and then ran across the lawn. The most amazing thing was that Gerald was not afraid.
There was still something white under the tree. Gerald moved closer and saw a pedestal for a statue. But nothing stood on it.
"The statues . . . ," he murmured. Just then another statue walked out of the Temple of Flora and disappeared into some bushes. "They come alive!"
Gerald heard the crunching sound of something walking along the gravel path. An enormous stone dinosaur was lumbering toward him!
"It can't see me," Gerald told himself. "I'm not afraid."
As the dinosaur passed, Gerald reached out and touched it. The moving statue turned toward him, but Gerald was suddenly afraid. He took off and ran toward the castle.

Gerald spotted the open window of the treasure room. He climbed up to the window, using the vine that clung to the castle. Once inside the room, he turned and looked outside. In the moonlight he could see that the goat-boy statue was back underneath the willow tree. Nothing moved outdoors.
"This is very strange. Maybe I'm dreaming."
He shut the window and removed the key from the door lock. Outside the treasure room, he locked the door again. Then he put the key in its hiding place and crept along the corridor.

He wandered through the castle, opening doors and feeling safe because he was invisible. At last he came to a door with light shining under it. Gerald hesitated for a moment before flinging open the door.
"Hey!" cried a voice from within the room.
Gerald flattened himself against the wall as a man sprang to the door. The man flashed a lantern into the corridor.
"It's all right," the man said. "It was only the door swinging open."
"Close that door!" growled another voice.
That was fine with Gerald. He had already seen enough. A gang of burglars was taking silver out of two large chests! They had picked the door's lock and now their tools lay on the floor.
"Hurry up!" one burglar said.
Gerald ran down the corridor. What should he do? He hurried outside. Through a window he saw Mabel and her aunt having a delicious supper.
He took out his notebook and pencil and wrote:
You know the room where the silver is? Burglars have picked the lock and are stealing the silver. Send a man for the police. A friend
P.S. This is not a joke.

Gerald looked hungrily at Mabel's supper. He tied the note to a rock with his shoelace. Then he threw the rock through the window. Mabel and her aunt jumped up, shrieking in surprise. Mabel picked up the rock, and her aunt read the note.
"Nonsense!" said the aunt. "Of course this is a joke."
"Please," wailed Mabel. "Send for the police like he says."
"Like who says?" snapped her aunt.
"Whoever wrote the note," moaned Mabel.
Gerald realized he must do something more. "Send for the police at once," he called out in his manliest voice. "You'll only blame yourself if you don't."
"Auntie, please wake Bates right away," begged Mabel.
"Oh, all right." Mabel's aunt finally went off to get one of the male servants.
Bates was not happy to be woken up. But after reading the note, he went to the police on his bicycle. By the time the police arrived, the burglars and the silver were gone.
Gerald had a long night. It was late when he crept into bed, exhausted and cold as stone.
The next morning Eliza the maid went into Gerald's room. "Wake up! It's a beautiful day!"
She opened the curtains at one window and turned to call him again. But his bed was empty.
"I wonder where he is." She opened the curtains at the other window.
But this time when she turned around, she screamed. Gerald was lying in the bed!
At the sound of the maid's scream, Kathleen ran into Gerald's room. "What's wrong?"

"One minute Gerald was gone!" said Eliza. "The next minute he was in the bed! I don't know what's wrong with me. Yesterday I was hearing voices, and now this." Eliza shook her head as she left the room.
"What happened?" Kathleen asked Gerald.
"The ring came off when Eliza called me. I'm hungry. I'll tell you everything later."
After breakfast Gerald remembered he'd left the ring in bed. But when he went upstairs, Eliza had already made his bed. He asked her about the ring.
"I didn't see anything," she said. "If there was a ring in the bed, I'd have seen it."
The children searched every corner of the room, but couldn't find the ring.
Soon they gave up because they had to meet Mabel in town. They sat on a wall to wait for her.

"Hey, you went back to normal faster than I did," Mabel said to Gerald. Now Gerald could tell the story of the three burglars. After throwing the rock, he'd returned to the room where they were loading their sacks. He'd followed the men out into the night and discovered their hiding place.
"Look, there's Officer Johnson," said Gerald. "I need to talk to him."
Gerald hopped off the wall and went over to Officer Johnson. "Would you like to catch those burglars who've been stealing silver?"
"What do you know about that?" Johnson asked suspiciously.
"I saw something last night, but I could get in trouble for being out late. Do you promise not to tell anyone?"
Johnson nodded.
"I saw three men taking silver from the castle. I know where they put it."
"So you wrote the note?" Johnson said eagerly.
"Yes." Gerald explained how he'd watched the men go down to the river. They had tied their bags of silver under a dock.
Tonight, after dark, they planned to retrieve the silver and escape by boat.
"You can catch them then," said Gerald.
"But which dock is their hiding spot?" asked Johnson.
"Follow me," said Gerald. "When I take out my handkerchief and blow my nose, that'll be the place."
Gerald went back to the other children. "Come on! Let's play follow-the-leader."

The children followed him, running and jumping and imitating his every step. Johnson followed at a distance. On one dock Gerald suddenly stopped and blew his nose. Then he led the children back to the school.
"We've brought our friend Mabel home for lunch," said Kathleen when Eliza opened the door. "Where's Mademoiselle?"
"She's gone to visit the castle. The grounds are open to the public today. Now hurry up with your lunch. This is my afternoon off. My fiancé doesn't like waiting for me."
The children ate quickly and Eliza left. "Where's the ring?" asked Mabel. "I really need to put it back."
"I haven't had a turn yet," protested Jimmy. "When we find it—"
" When you find it?" said Mabel.
They told her about losing the ring. "Oh no!" cried Mabel. "We have to find it!"
The children searched and searched Gerald's room, but they still couldn't find the ring.

Suddenly there was pounding at the back door. Kathleen ran downstairs. A strange man stood near the doorstep. His eyes were open wide with amazement. One arm was stretched out toward the door. The rest of him looked as if he were trying to run the other way. "Let go of me!" he cried.
"I won't let go of you!" said Eliza's voice. But no Eliza could be seen.
The children quickly realized that the strange man at the door was Eliza's fiancé. And that an invisible Eliza was holding his hand tightly.
"He keeps saying he can't see me," said Eliza's voice.
"Well, I can't," protested her fiancé.
"I know you have the ring," Gerald whispered to Eliza. "Go inside."
"What's going on?" asked the man, who seemed to relax once Eliza released him. "Have I been acting strange?"
"Very strange," said Mabel.
"You should go home and lie down," said Gerald. "The sun is very hot today."
"Yes . . . yes . . . ," the man said with a puzzled look. "I'll do that."
Once he was gone, the children went inside to talk to Eliza. It took a while to convince her that she really was invisible. She said she'd found the ring in the bed and "borrowed" it.
"Do I have to stay like this?" she wailed. "No man will marry a girl he can't see."
"It doesn't last forever," said Mabel kindly.
"And we'll help you," added Kathleen.
"Now let's get Mademoiselle's tea ready," said Gerald.
"And ours!" said Jimmy.
"No." Gerald looked thoughtful. "We'll have a picnic and take Eliza. I'll go get some cakes."
While Gerald was out, Mademoiselle came home from visiting the castle. She seemed tired and a little sad.
As soon as Gerald returned, the children and Eliza started for the castle. They watched the sun go down as they had their picnic on the castle grounds.
"I should go home now," said Mabel.
"Well, I can't go home like this," said Eliza. She pointed to a white marble temple. "I'd live in that little white house over there if it had any walls."
"Oh, you mean the Temple of Apollo," said Mabel.
"What a lot of steps to clean!" said Eliza. "Why do they make houses without walls? Who'd live in . . ." She paused. "What's that?"
"What?" asked Kathleen and Jimmy together. They couldn't see anything.
"That white thing coming down the steps," said Eliza. "Oh! It's a young man. But he looks like a statue."
"I thought I saw the statues come alive last night!" exclaimed Gerald. "I think it happens after sunset."
" I never saw them come alive," said Mabel. "And I've often been in the gardens at night."
"I know I saw them moving," said Gerald.
"I believe you," said Mabel. "I wonder if you can only see them move when you're invisible."
"You're probably right," Gerald replied.
"Oh look!" said Eliza. "There's another statue! He's got little wings on his feet!"
"That's probably Hermes, the messenger of the gods," said Gerald.
"What are you talking about?" asked Jimmy. "I don't see any moving statues."
The gardens stretched in front of the children. They could only see the statues standing still. But Eliza could see statues walking over the lawn and swimming in the lake.
"Oh, here's a dear little boy," she said. "He's coming right toward me."
The next moment she was screaming. There was the sound of boots on gravel—Eliza was running away!

"She must have touched the statue!" cried Gerald. "Then she became afraid, just like I did last night. Come on," he added. "We have to catch her before she frightens everybody in town with her screams."

Mabel stayed at the castle, but the others ran as fast as they could. They didn't catch up with Eliza until they reached their own back door. Just as the church clock struck the half-hour, Eliza suddenly reappeared.
She held out her hand. The magic ring was on her finger.
The next morning the three children decided to walk to town. Soon they ran into Mabel. Gerald knew she was going to ask about the ring. Luckily they'd gotten it back from Eliza the previous night.
Every Friday a market was set up in the square. Vendors sold chickens, vegetables, toys, and all sorts of interesting things.
"Let's buy some flowers for Mademoiselle," suggested Kathleen.
"Yes," agreed Gerald. "We haven't paid attention to her for the longest time."
The children chose three bunches of carnations. Then they went back to the school.
Gerald knocked on the door of the sitting room, where Mademoiselle spent all her days. The other children gathered behind him.
"With love from all of us." Gerald gave the flowers to her.
Mademoiselle kissed him on both cheeks.
"What are you painting?" asked Jimmy.
"The castle."
"That's very good," said Mabel.
"Are you a friend from town?" Mademoiselle asked her.
"Actually I live at Yalding Towers," said Mabel, using the castle's formal name.
That name seemed to impress Mademoiselle. "Are you part of Lord Yalding's family?"
"No, he doesn't have any family. He's not married. I'm his housekeeper's niece."
"But you know him, don't you?" asked Mademoiselle.
"No, I've never seen him. But he's supposed to be coming soon."
"Why doesn't he live there?" Mademoiselle seemed very interested in this man.
"My aunt says he's too poor," said Mabel. She explained that the castle had originally belonged to Lord Yalding's uncle. Lord Yalding had wanted to marry a woman, but his uncle had not allowed it.

"She was a ballerina or something," explained Mabel. When the uncle died, he left his castle to Lord Yalding. But he left his money to a cousin. So Lord Yalding didn't have enough money to live at the castle. Meanwhile the woman Lord Yalding loved was sent away to a convent.
"Did he ever try to find her?" asked Mademoiselle.
"Oh yes," said Mabel. "But there are so many convents." Her eyes glowed brightly. "Still, I believe he will find her one day."
Mademoiselle stared silently at Mabel. "My goodness!" she said finally. "You know a lot about Lord Yalding! You're a very nice girl. Why don't you stay for lunch?"
Mademoiselle went out to buy some special treats. Jimmy and Kathleen set the dining room table. Gerald and Mabel were left in the sitting room.
"You know," Gerald suddenly said. "It's lucky those burglars didn't go after the jewels in the treasure room."
"I don't think anyone knows about those jewels except the four of us," said Mabel. "Anyway, if the burglars do know, it'll all come out at the trial."
"There won't be a trial," said Gerald.
"What do you mean?"
"After I told Officer Johnson where to find the silver, I started thinking. I visited a prison once with my father. It was awful!"

Gerald didn't want to be responsible for sending someone to prison. So he had left the burglars a note, warning them about the police. But he also said if they didn't stop stealing, he'd make sure they went to jail.
"Speaking of stealing," said Mabel, "did you get the ring back from Eliza?"
"Yes, but I don't know if it'll make you invisible again."
"Why not? Did you do something to it?" Mabel asked sharply.
"No, but it seems to be losing its powers. You were invisible for 21 hours. I was invisible for 14, and Eliza for 7. Next time it might not work at all."
Mabel shook her head. "We don't understand the mystery of that ring yet."
The children had a delightful lunch with Mademoiselle. She served them cakes and tarts, and made wreaths for their heads. She drew pictures and told stories about her own school days.
"Draw us a picture of a theater," said Gerald.
"Do you like plays?" asked Mabel.
"Oh yes, I love them!" Mademoiselle concentrated on her drawing.
The children looked at each other and smiled.
"We'll put on a play for you tonight," said Jimmy.
"And please, may Eliza come too?" asked Kathleen.
"Of course," said Mademoiselle with a smile.

Mademoiselle stayed in the sitting room as usual. It was a good thing that she was not trying to concentrate! The children came in and out all afternoon, asking for things. May they have the sofa cushions? May they have the clothesline? Did she have any brightly colored scarves they could borrow? May they have tea in the garden because the stage was in the dining room?

At last Eliza rang the dinner bell. That was the signal for Mademoiselle to go into the dining room for the play. Several tables had been pushed together to make a stage. Rows of chairs were set out for an audience.
Mademoiselle was surprised to see seven people sitting in these chairs. "Children," she whispered through the stage curtains. "You should have asked me before you invited guests."
The children laughed. "Turn up the lights," said Mabel.
Mademoiselle looked again at the people in the audience. "Oh! They're not alive!" she cried in surprise.

And indeed they were not. Their bodies were made of pillows and rolled-up blankets. Their spines were broom handles. Their arms and legs were hockey sticks and umbrellas. They were dressed in whatever coats, hats, and gloves the children could find. And their faces were paper masks made by Gerald.
"You've made yourself an audience! Bravo!" said Mademoiselle. And she and Eliza clapped.
They sat down and the curtain opened. " Beauty and the Beast ," announced a voice from backstage.
The children had spent much time making their costumes and audience. So they'd had little time to rehearse. But they had fun acting out the fairy tale.
As Beauty, Mabel wore her princess clothes. As the Beast, Gerald wore some small rugs. Jimmy and Kathleen played all the minor parts.
At the end of the second scene, everyone was backstage.
"You should give me the ring," Mabel said to Gerald.
He'd forgotten that it was in his pocket. "I'll do it in the next scene."
And he did, making the ring part of the play. He told Beauty that the ring was a magic ring. It would give her anything she wished. So to see him again, she simply had to put it on and make her wish.
At last they came to the final scene. Beauty was reunited with Beast, who was really a prince. Mademoiselle and Eliza clapped and cheered.
Mabel looked at the fake audience members. "I wish those creatures we made were alive. We'd get some real applause then."
"I'm glad they aren't alive," said Gerald. "I feel silly when I look at them."

And suddenly it happened. There was the sound of more clapping. Seven paper faces were looking eagerly up at the stage. The creatures had come alive! Mademoiselle and Eliza screamed and ran from the room.
"Give me the ring!" Gerald said to Mabel.
He put the ring on his finger and cried, "I wish those Ugly-Wuglies weren't alive!" But nothing changed.
Mabel and Gerald followed the creatures out into the hallway. "Excuse me," one said to Gerald, "can you recommend a good hotel?"
Gerald didn't know what to say to the Ugly-Wugly. "You want a hotel?" he finally said.
"A good hotel," said the middle-aged gentleman.
"I'm sorry, but the hotels here shut early. They're all closed now."
Gerald had said the first thing that came into his head. He couldn't send these creatures to a real hotel. They'd frighten everyone in town!
"What about a lodging house?" asked a lady in a bonnet.
Another lady pushed her way to the front of the group. "Where are the carriages that we ordered?"
"I don't know, but I'll find out," said Gerald, pretending everything was normal. "We'd better get going now. The play is over. It's time to close the building and put out the lights."
"Let's get going," repeated the gentleman, who seemed to be the leader of the group. He stepped toward the front door.
"I can go with you and help you find a place to stay," said Gerald. "But you'll have to wait a few moments in the backyard."
The Ugly-Wuglies grumbled. For some reason they didn't like that idea.
"It's a very nice backyard," Gerald said. "The pump was just painted green."
The Ugly-Wuglies seemed interested in the fresh paint. Gerald led them out into the backyard. He hoped no one would see them.

"I hate to make you wait," he said, inventing an excuse. "But my uncle is quite insane. I have to give him his supper now. When he sees strangers—even nice ones like you—he gets quite upset. So please wait right here."
"Perhaps we should try to find a hotel ourselves?" the lady in the bonnet said nervously.
"Oh no," Gerald said, acting very serious. "The police arrest all strangers. It's a new law."
As Gerald went back into the school, he heard the creatures muttering. They said things like "quite the polite young gentleman."
Although the creatures looked horrible, Gerald wasn't afraid. He knew it was because he was wearing the ring. As long as he didn't touch them, he could be brave.
He found the other children in the dining room. He didn't want them to be afraid.
"This is such fun!" he said in a cheerful voice. "The Ugly-Wuglies are just like real people. They're quite kind and jolly."
"Fun?" Kathleen said doubtfully.
Gerald told them about the need for a hotel. "Wait here while I go up to talk to Mademoiselle and Eliza."
He ran upstairs.
"I wonder what lies he's telling them," said Jimmy.
Gerald came down again and said that he'd walk Mabel home.
"What about a hotel for the Ugly-Wuglies?" she reminded him.
"Is there a place on the castle grounds? I need to put them somewhere until the charm breaks," said Gerald. "Then they'll just be a pack of coats and things. And we can carry those home later."
"There's a secret passage in the Temple of Flora," said Mabel.
Right then an Ugly-Wugly opened the back door. He looked in anxiously.
"We'd better go," said Gerald.
He went outside with Mabel. "This is my friend Mabel. She played the princess in the play."
The middle-aged Ugly-Wugly shook her hand.
The one in the bonnet took Mabel's arm. "You clever thing. Do walk with me."

And so they walked through town like any other group of people. Mabel had to keep telling herself that the creatures weren't real. They passed only one man who stared at them. But he just muttered to himself.
At last they reached the gates to the castle grounds. Gerald tried to open the gates, but couldn't. They were locked.
The Ugly-Wuglies shook the gates in front of the castle. "It's late," Gerald explained. "There's another way into this hotel. But you have to climb through a hole."
"The ladies won't like that," said the middle-aged gentleman.
But the ladies said they loved adventures. "Such a thrill!" said the one in the hat with flowers.

So they went along the road until they came to the hole in the bushes. Gerald went first with a lantern. Next it was Mabel's turn. Then all the creatures slid down into the cave. They followed Gerald into the arched tunnel and out onto the terrace.
"Oh!" The creatures admired the view in the moonlight. They continued along the gravel paths toward the Temple of Flora. Gerald's plan was to hide the creatures in the passage until the charm broke.
Suddenly Gerald saw the statue of Hermes leap from his pedestal. Gerald was still wearing the ring. He knew that he was the only one who could see Hermes coming toward them.
Gerald slipped the ring from his finger. The statue was back on its pedestal, still as could be. When Gerald put the ring back on, Hermes was circling the Ugly-Wuglies.
"This is a very superior hotel," said an Ugly-Wugly wearing a top hat. "The grounds are beautiful."
"We'll have to enter through the back door," Mabel said. "The front door is locked early."
"What an adventure!" muttered a short Ugly-Wugly in a cap. "I feel young again!"
They hurried up the steps of the Temple of Flora. Mabel went behind the statue of the goddess. Gerald's lantern lit up a door.
"This way," said Mabel.
"You lead the way," said the middle-aged gentleman to Gerald.
"Uh . . . I . . . I must stay behind to close the door," said Gerald. "You wouldn't want us to get in trouble, would you?"
The creatures agreed they didn't want that.
"Here, you take the lantern." Gerald handed it to the middle-aged gentleman. "I wish you a pleasant stay in the very nice hotel."
One by one the other creatures followed their leader into the passage. Waiting outside, Mabel and Gerald hardly dared to breathe.
But before they could shut the door, there was a scuffling noise. The creatures were trying to escape!
Mabel and Gerald struggled to close the door.
"Oh, I can't push anymore!" cried Mabel.
"They mustn't get out!" said Gerald.
"What's going on?" said a new voice behind the children.
"Help us!" cried Gerald.
A man stepped in and helped the children shut the door.
"Thank you," said Mabel breathlessly. "Who are you?"
"I've come from London." The man paused. "To be the caretaker of this estate. Now tell me what this is all about. Who were those strange people?"
"If we told you the truth, you wouldn't believe us," said Gerald.
"Remember, I saw them," said the man.
"Tell him," Mabel urged Gerald.
So Gerald told the whole story of the magic ring. "We think the creatures will turn back into old coats tomorrow. Then we can take them home. Do you believe any of this?"
"No." The man shook his head.
It was time for the children to go home. "Don't open that door," Gerald warned the man. "Wait for us to come back tomorrow at ten o'clock."
The next morning the four children returned to the Temple of Flora. Everything was quiet.
"Look!" Kathleen cried. She pointed to the floor. The caretaker lay there, moaning softly.
At the same time, an Ugly-Wugly was peering at them through the bushes.
The creature's face disappeared into the bushes. The children bent over the caretaker.
"He's not dead, is he?" Jimmy asked anxiously.
"Just hurt," said Kathleen. "He's very handsome, don't you think?"
"Oh yes," agreed Mabel.
"Quite a nice young man," said a voice behind them.

The children looked up. And there was the middle-aged Ugly-Wugly. Everyone but Gerald screamed. He was still wearing the ring, so he wasn't afraid. But he noticed something strange. The middle-aged Ugly-Wugly's face was no longer made of paper—it was real. And so were his arms and legs. Somehow this creature had really come alive!
"What happened to the caretaker?" Gerald asked him.
"It was most unfortunate," said the Ugly-Wugly. "The others must have lost their way in the passage last night. They never found the hotel."
"Did you find it?" Gerald said in surprise.

"Of course. I wandered through the passage until I found the very nice hotel, just as you said. When I found the others again, they were behind this door. They were angry. They'd been here all night, trying to get out."
Jimmy's eyes were wide with fear.
"Here, take the ring," Gerald whispered. Jimmy put on the ring and instantly looked braver.
"But what happened to the caretaker?" Gerald asked again.
"He suddenly opened the door. Before I could protect him, the man in the top hat hit him. I was just going for help when you arrived."
"We must find the others," said Gerald.
"They've gone to bathe in the lake," said the Ugly-Wugly. "Their clothes are in the woods."
Kathleen and Jimmy went to check on the other Ugly-Wuglies. Gerald and Mabel stayed behind to tend to the caretaker. The Ugly-Wugly sat down on the temple steps.
In the woods Jimmy found four heaps of clothing. There were broomsticks, hockey sticks, and masks. All these things had made up the Ugly-Wugly men.
Kathleen found the two ladies sitting on a bench in the sun. But they had no life in them. Jimmy shook them to pieces.
"The spell is broken." Kathleen sighed with relief.
They went back to the Temple of Flora. The caretaker was trying to sit up.
Gerald told the Ugly-Wugly to hide in the bushes so he wouldn't frighten the caretaker.
"Jimmy is the best one to go with you," said Gerald. That was true because Jimmy had the ring.
The children helped the caretaker to his feet.
"Are you sure you're all right?" Mabel asked him.
"Yes. But I had the strangest dream." He looked around. "I'm grateful for your help. You may visit here whenever you like."
They all shook hands, and the caretaker walked away.
"We have to get rid of that Ugly-Wugly," said Kathleen.
"But how?" asked Gerald. "He became real inside the passage. If we could just get him back there . . ."
Suddenly Jimmy came out of the bushes.
"The Ugly-Wugly is taking a walk," Jimmy said. "He says he's a very rich businessman and he needs to get to London."
Gerald and the girls were still planning how to get rid of the Ugly-Wugly. But Jimmy wasn't paying attention.
"He has a car and a tennis court. I wish I were rich," said Jimmy. "I'd spend my money on . . ."
"Oh no!" cried the girls, looking at Jimmy.
Suddenly he was growing rich right in front of them. But he was also growing older. When the changes stopped, the girls gasped.
"Do you know the way to the train station?" asked rich, old Jimmy.
Kathleen burst into tears at the sight of Jimmy as an old man.
"Don't cry, little girl," said Jimmy.
The children quickly realized that he didn't know them anymore.
The middle-aged Ugly-Wugly approached Jimmy. The two men seemed to recognize each other. They started to walk away.
"Oh no!" said Kathleen. "Where are they going? What will happen to Jimmy when the spell breaks?"
"Don't worry," said Gerald. "I'll follow Jimmy. Clean up the Ugly-Wuglies and then go home. You can tell Mademoiselle that Jimmy and I are with an uncle."
Kathleen and Mabel gathered up the pile of old clothes, hockey sticks, and brooms. That was all that was left of the six Ugly-Wuglies.
"Let's hide them in the stone dinosaur," said Mabel. "He's hollow."
"Then we can have a nice tea party with our dolls," said Kathleen. "That'll make us forget all about this magic."
The girls hid everything in the belly of the dinosaur. Then they returned to the school for tea. But Kathleen couldn't forget about the magic. She was still worried about her brothers.
Meanwhile Gerald got on the train. He followed Jimmy and the Ugly-Wugly to London. Then he followed them into an office building.
On one door it said, "Mr. U. W. Ugli, Stockbroker." On the next floor, Gerald saw a door with Jimmy's name on it. He didn't know what to do. So he sat on the stairs.
A messenger boy came down the steps, whistling. "What are you doing here?" he asked Gerald.
"Uh . . . I'm a detective. What do you know about Mr. Ugli?"
"He's awfully rich," said the boy.
"And what about that other man upstairs?"
"He's even richer! Those two are rivals. Why are you so interested in them?"
Gerald had to think up an excuse. "That man upstairs is wanted by his family. I need to get him out of his office."
"I think Mr. Ugli would be glad to be rid of him for a day or two. Go in and ask him for help."
With that, the messenger boy left Gerald on the stairs. After a few minutes of thinking, Gerald came up with a plan. He went into Mr. Ugli's office and talked to him.

At lunchtime Mr. Ugli and Jimmy went out to a restaurant. Gerald followed them and sat at a table nearby. The restaurant was crowded and noisy. But Gerald could still hear Mr. Ugli asking about the ring.
"Oh yes, this is a family treasure," said Jimmy.
"May I look more closely at it?" asked Mr. Ugli.
Then he took the ring from Jimmy's finger. And he dropped it. Just as Gerald and Mr. Ugli had planned!
Gerald pounced on the ring. He put it on his own finger and made a wish.
"I wish Jimmy and I were inside the secret passage in the Temple of Flora."
It was the first safe place he could think of.
Gerald felt dizzy. Everything was very dark. How was he going to deal with Jimmy until the spell wore off?
But there was no need to worry. "Gerald! Are you awake? I had such a strange dream."
Jimmy had returned to normal.
"It's that ring again," said Gerald. "I had to wish us here to get you out of your dream."
"Where are we?"
"In the passage behind the Temple of Flora."
"But how are we going to get out?" asked Jimmy.
"I'll wish us out, of course," said Gerald.
So he wished but nothing happened. He handed the ring to Jimmy in the darkness. Jimmy wished and nothing happened. The boys were trapped.
Kathleen and Mabel were still at their tea party. Suddenly they both felt the same way. They must go to the Temple of Flora! They didn't know why, but they knew they must go.

When Gerald and Jimmy yelled for help, Kathleen and Mabel were ready to help. The girls opened the door, and the boys were free. Kathleen hugged her brothers. They spoke about their adventures in London and in the secret passage.
"Did you leave that Ugly-Wugly in London?" asked Mabel.
"Yes," said Gerald. "Now we'll seal the ring in an envelope so no one else gets in trouble."
"But I didn't have a chance to use it," protested Kathleen.
"You've seen what it does," said Gerald. "Why would you want to use it?"
"I'd make it do nice things," said Kathleen.
"Let's just put it back in the treasure room," said Mabel. "It was a bad idea to take it."
They walked over to the castle. In the treasure room, Mabel pushed the secret button. The panels slid up. All the jewels sparkled on the shelves. Mabel took the ring from Gerald.
"I don't even know what to call that ring," said Kathleen. "The wishing ring? The invisibility ring?"
"Oh!" Mabel put the ring on. "I understand now. The ring is whatever you say it is. It made us invisible because I said that's what it does. Then it became a wishing ring during our play."
"It's still a wishing ring," said Jimmy.
"No," said Mabel. "We've already had that. I say it's a ring that makes the wearer four meters high."
She was still wearing the ring. Even as she spoke, she started to grow. Soon she was four meters high. But she didn't grow much in width. So she was very, very skinny.
"Oh, Mabel, that was silly," said Kathleen. "Who knows how long this spell will last?"
"What am I going to do now?" moaned Mabel.
"We must hide you until you're back to your right size," said Gerald. "How about in an empty room?"
"I'd rather stay outside," said Mabel. "It's a good thing my aunt thinks I'm staying overnight with you."
The children went outside. Mabel had to crawl to fit through doors. Outside she crept behind some bushes so no one would see her.
"Aren't you hungry?" asked Jimmy.
"Oh yes," said Mabel. "I'll write to my aunt, and she'll send us a picnic."
Mabel used Gerald's notebook to write a note.
Dear Aunt,
May we have some things for a picnic? Gerald will bring them. I'd come myself, but I'm tired. I think I've been growing rather fast.
Your loving niece,
Mabel
Gerald went to fetch the food. When he came back, they had a splendid picnic of bread, cake, gooseberries, and milk.
Gerald noticed the dinosaur statue nearby. "He must have eaten some good meals in his time."
Kathleen giggled. "We fed him today."
"What do you mean?" asked Jimmy.
Kathleen explained how she and Mabel had hidden the Ugly-Wuglies' clothes in the dinosaur's belly.
"We can take them home now," said Gerald.
"I've got an idea," Kathleen suddenly said. "Give me the ring."
She ran ahead of the others. "I say this is a wishing ring." She believed the ring would change if she renamed it.
When they reached the dinosaur, Kathleen climbed up into its belly. She handed down the clothes and other Ugly-Wugly things to her brothers.
"Wait a minute," said Gerald. "I'm coming up."
"Isn't it nice in here?" said Kathleen. "I wish I were a statue. Oh!"
And just like that, Kathleen turned into a statue.
Kathleen had turned completely white and still. Gerald was so shocked, he could not speak. His sister was now made of marble.
At last he called down to Jimmy. "Kathleen made the ring a wishing ring again. Then she wished she was a statue."
"And is she?" asked Jimmy.
"Come up and look."
Jimmy climbed into the dinosaur. "She's really a statue," he said. "Let's go tell Mabel."
Mabel was still hiding in the bushes. The boys told her about Kathleen. Mabel gasped. "What will happen next?"
"She'll go back to normal," said Gerald.
"But what about me?" said Mabel. "You don't know how frightening it is to be out here like this. Can't you get the ring?"
"It may have turned to stone, but I'll try," said Gerald.
Gerald climbed back into the dinosaur. The ring had not turned to marble.
"I'm sorry, Kathleen." He took the ring.
Then he gave it to Mabel. "Now you won't be afraid of anything."
Mabel wanted to be closer to the dinosaur. Then she would be near Kathleen when her spell broke.
After she crawled over to the dinosaur, she stood up and looked inside.
"It'll be all right," she reassured Kathleen. "I'm nearby. Call me when you feel yourself getting better."
Inside her marble shell, Kathleen heard Mabel. But she couldn't speak.

The boys covered Mabel with the Ugly-Wuglies' clothes so she'd stay warm. They promised to return later to check on the girls. Then they went back to the school. They told Mademoiselle that Kathleen was staying overnight with Mabel.
The sun set and the moon rose. Mabel fell asleep. Inside the dinosaur Kathleen knew she must wait patiently for her own spell to break. Soon she fell asleep.
Kathleen woke up suddenly in the middle of the night. The dinosaur was moving!
"Oh, how dreadful!" she said. "The dinosaur must have come alive in the moonlight. That's what Gerald said happened to the statues."
She was afraid to drop through the hole while the statue moved. But where was Mabel? What if the dinosaur stepped on her?
Kathleen peered through the hole. The dinosaur was moving faster. The floor of its stomach sloped downward. They were going downhill.
Through the hole Kathleen saw grass and then stone. She heard the splash of water. They were near the lake. The dinosaur was about to go swimming!
Kathleen jumped through the hole just as the dinosaur reached the lake. She raced into the Temple of Apollo.
"Be still, little lady," said a voice. "I leap."
Kathleen watched as the statue of Apollo leaped from the pedestal.
"You're new here," said Apollo.
"I'm quite new," said Kathleen. "I didn't know you could talk."
"Why not? You can."
"But I'm alive," said Kathleen.
"And so am I," said the statue.
"I suppose so. But I thought I'd need the ring to see you."
"That's for mortals. We statues can hear and see each other."
At that, Apollo dove into the lake. Kathleen wanted to get Mabel and go home. She found Mabel sleeping under the pile of Ugly-Wugly clothing.
"Wake up!" she called.
"I want to go home," said Mabel.
"So do I, but you can't go home like that. You're still too tall."
Mabel closed her eyes. "Oh, Kathleen, I feel so funny. Am I shrinking?"
"Yes!" said Kathleen. "Now we can go home."
"But what about you?"
"What do you mean? I'm fine," said Kathleen.
"Look at yourself."
Kathleen looked down at her hands and her dress. "Why am I this horrid color?" she cried.
"Don't you understand?" asked Mabel. "You're still a statue!"
"You've come alive with the other statues in the moonlight," Mabel gently explained to Kathleen.
"Why aren't you afraid of me?" asked Kathleen.
"I have the ring," said Mabel. "Maybe we can find out more about this magic place. That is, if the other statues will talk to us."
"Apollo was very nice," said Kathleen. "He's swimming in the lake now."
The girls walked to the lake and sat on the grass to wait for Apollo.
"Hello, little sister," said Apollo, emerging from the lake. "Who's your friend?"
"This is Mabel," said Kathleen.
"How can you see us, and why aren't you afraid?" asked Apollo.
Mabel showed him the ring.
"Now I understand. You should become a statue and swim with us."
"I can't swim," said Mabel.
"Me neither," said Kathleen.
" You can swim," Apollo said to Kathleen. "All statues that come to life are excellent swimmers." Again he urged Mabel to become a statue.
"This ring . . . ," she said hesitantly. "You wish for things and you never know how long they'll last."
Apollo explained that she must set a time limit on the ring's powers.
"We'll swim to the island and feast with the gods," he said.
"Oh, I'm so hungry!" said Kathleen. "Do it, Mabel!"
So Mabel decided to become a statue. First she removed her shoes and stockings. She didn't think they'd look nice in marble!
Then she said, "I wish I could be a statue of living marble until dawn. After that I want to return to normal."
Mabel turned into a statue. Apollo and the girls ran to the lake and jumped in.
The girls were delighted that they could swim with ease.
When they reached the island, Apollo led them to a pool.
All around the pool were statues of gods and goddesses. And they were all alive. Some were dancing. Some were splashing their feet in the pool.
Apollo introduced the girls. A goddess placed a wreath on everyone's head. Then the feast began.
A young woman named Psyche handed them ripe pomegranates.
"I wish the boys were here!" Kathleen said.
"I wonder what they're doing," said Mabel.
Hermes landed on the grass. "They climbed out a window, and now they're looking for you."
"It's easy to wish them here," said Apollo.
Kathleen took the ring. "I wish the boys could be statues of living marble until dawn. Afterward I want them to return to normal."
"You should have wished them here ," said Apollo. "But Hermes will fetch them and explain everything to them."
He held up the ring. "The ring is the heart of the magic." Then he gave the ring back to Kathleen.
"We don't usually question guests," said Hera, the queen of the gods. "But everyone is interested in your ring. How did you get it?"
Just then the boys arrived. They hugged the girls. They feasted. Then Mabel told the story of the ring.
"How do you come alive?" Gerald asked Apollo.

"All statues can do it in the moonlight," said Apollo. "You've seen us because you wore the ring. But on one night of the year, anyone can see us in certain temples. One of those temples is in this great garden."
Then Apollo picked up a lyre. Kathleen leaned against Psyche as Apollo played. The music was so beautiful that everyone felt at peace.
Then suddenly Apollo cried, "Dawn is coming! To your pedestals!"
The gods leaped up and ran away.
"What's the secret of the ring?" Mabel called after them.
"Ask at the Temple of Strange Stones in five days," said Hermes as he flew away.
The sun rose, and the children were no longer statues. They were standing knee-deep in brambles and grass. The lawn, the marble steps, and the pool had disappeared. It was very cold.
"We're on the island," said Mabel. "But we can't swim anymore. We're stuck here."
"Isn't there a boat somewhere?" Jimmy asked.
"No." Mabel shivered.
"There must be something we can do," said Gerald.
"The ring!" cried Mabel. "We can wish ourselves home. Do you have the ring, Kathleen?"
Kathleen shook her head. "Psyche wanted to see it so I gave it to her. It's probably still on her finger!"
Everyone tried not to be angry with Kathleen. But everyone was upset.
"Maybe we can find Psyche's statue and get the ring back," said Gerald.
"I've never seen that statue," said Mabel.
Kathleen sniffled. She was about to cry.
"Why don't we explore the island," said Gerald. "Maybe we'll find a boat."
None of them believed that they'd find a boat. But they set off to explore the island anyway.
They were all miserable. The brambles scratched Mabel's bare feet and legs. She had left her shoes and stockings on the mainland.
"Come on, everybody, cheer up," said Gerald. "We'll get out of here."
Suddenly he stumbled and disappeared with a yell. Mabel nearly fell too. Right in front of her was a flight of moss-covered steps.
"Gerald, are you hurt?" she called down the steps.
"A little," he said. "But I found a passage."
"There's always a passage in this place," said Jimmy.
"I forgot about that passage!" declared Mabel. "It goes under the water and comes out at the Temple of Flora! Maybe it even goes past the place where the Ugly-Wugly found his good hotel."
"I'm not going down there in the dark," said Kathleen.
Gerald came back up the steps. "Maybe there's a secret spring."

Then Gerald led the way down the steps. He held Kathleen's hand so she wouldn't feel afraid. The steps led to a passage, which took a turn. Then there were more steps. These led to a straight, clean, marble passage.

Suddenly the children found themselves in a great hall. The room was filled with light. And each one of them noticed something different in the arches around the room. There was a ship at sea. A king on his throne. The Ugly-Wugly sitting happily in front of a good hotel.
"Oh, I'm glad we came!" said Kathleen.
They walked slowly through the hall. At the end of the hall, they saw the source of the light: the statue of Psyche. On its hand was the ring.
"I hope you don't mind," Gerald said to the statue. He removed the ring very gently.
They passed Psyche and entered a dark, twisting passage.
"Give me the ring, Gerald," said Kathleen. "I know what to say."
Gerald handed it to her reluctantly.
"I wish," she said slowly, "that no one at home will know we've been out tonight. I wish we were safe in our own beds and asleep."
And that is exactly what happened next.
Mabel was supposed to be sleeping at Kathleen's. And Kathleen was supposed to be sleeping at Mabel's. Mademoiselle and Mabel's aunt were surprised when the girls woke up in their own homes.
But somehow the girls managed to explain away the adults' questions. Neither the aunt nor Mademoiselle was angry. That was good because Kathleen and her brothers wanted to visit the castle that day.
Once again the castle grounds were open to the public. This time the castle was open too. There were more visitors than usual. Everyone in town had heard that Lord Yalding was coming.
"This isn't very much fun," complained Gerald, watching the crowd. "I hate to see all these people in our garden."
"I said that to the nice caretaker this morning," said Mabel. "But he didn't seem to mind all the people."
"Did you say anything else?" asked Jimmy.
"Lots more," said Mabel. "He's a good listener. I told him all about our adventures with the ring."
"You didn't!" said Gerald.
"Don't worry. He thought I was making everything up. He told me I should be a writer when I grow up."
"Let's do something with the ring," said Kathleen.
"We can't," said Gerald. "Mademoiselle said she's coming to meet us."
"But the caretaker said he'd make a picnic for us after everyone left," said Mabel. "We're supposed to meet him at five o'clock."
"Then you go meet him, and I'll wait for Mademoiselle," said Gerald. "I don't want you to miss the picnic."
So at five o'clock, Mabel, Kathleen, and Jimmy went to meet the caretaker. It was a very hot day, and they were grumpy.
They soon saw the caretaker near the edge of some woods. Two picnic baskets lay on the ground.
"I'm making tea," he said. "There's a little canal just over the ridge. You can go wading until the tea is ready."
The water was delightfully cool. Soon the children were in better spirits. And they were even happier when they had their tea. Such a feast of cakes and fruit!
"This is like the feast of the gods," said Jimmy.
"What are you talking about?" asked the caretaker.
Jimmy told him how they had turned into statues and eaten with the gods on the island.
"What big imaginations you all have!" said the caretaker.
"But everything I told you is true," Jimmy insisted. "And Mabel told you the truth about the ring too. Kathleen, give me the ring."
Kathleen reluctantly handed him the ring.
"This is the ring Mabel told you about," said Jimmy. "I say it's a wishing ring. If you wear it and make a wish, your wish will come true."
He gave the ring to the caretaker.
"Don't wish for anything silly," said Kathleen.
"I'll wish for the only thing I really want," said the caretaker. He closed his eyes. "I wish that my friend was here."
The three children expected to see a man appear. But they only saw Gerald and Mademoiselle coming toward them.
"Hello," said Gerald. "I persuaded Mademoiselle . . ."
He stopped talking because Mademoiselle and the caretaker were staring at each other.
"It's you!" said the caretaker.
"And you!" said Mademoiselle in an odd, choked voice.
"Is she your friend?" asked Jimmy.
"Yes," said the caretaker. "Jimmy, give your brother some tea. Mademoiselle, please come walk with me. I have so much to say to you."
"We'll be back in an hour," said Mademoiselle, who suddenly looked younger and more beautiful. "It has been a long time since Lord Yalding and I have seen each other."
The children watched Mademoiselle and Lord Yalding walk away.
"So the caretaker is Lord Yalding!" said Jimmy. "And Mademoiselle is his friend."
"She's not his friend !" Mabel said scornfully. "She's the lady he wanted to marry, but his uncle wouldn't let him. She's the one who was sent to the convent!"
"And now the ring has brought them together," said Kathleen.
"I wonder if they'll be married tomorrow," said Mabel.
"Wouldn't it be fun if we were bridesmaids?" said Kathleen.
"I think Mademoiselle is very lucky." Mabel sighed.
Mademoiselle was also very happy.
Years ago her guardian had put her in the convent. He'd said he didn't want her to lose her fortune by marrying a poor lord.
But he had really wanted her fortune for himself. So he'd stolen all her money and run off to South America. And she'd been left with nothing.

Mademoiselle had had to work in order to live. She'd taken the job at Kathleen's school because it was near Lord Yalding's home. She still loved him even though she thought he didn't love her anymore. She didn't know that he had been looking for her all this time.

The day after the picnic, Lord Yalding came to the school. He took everyone back to the castle in a wagon pulled by two fine horses. The children wanted to explore the castle. Mabel showed them all the secret doors and secret passages and secret stairs.
They ate lunch in the great hall. It was where Mabel had first served them bread and cheese. This time they ate a real meal served on silver dishes.
Gerald raised his glass of lemonade for a toast: "To Lord and Lady Yalding."
Mademoiselle's eyes were bright with tears of happiness.
"And by the way . . . ," Gerald said to Lord Yalding. "I know you don't believe in the ring, but we do. May we have it back?"
Lord Yalding handed him the ring.

But Lord Yalding and Mademoiselle could not be completely happy yet. They had found each other, but they could not afford to live in the castle. They talked of renting it to someone rich. But they didn't know anyone with enough money.
"I have an idea," said Jimmy. "Why don't you sell your jewels?"
"What jewels?" said Lord Yalding. "I don't have any jewels."
"I mean the ones in the paneled room with the stars on the ceiling. There are shelves and shelves of beautiful family jewels. You could sell them and . . ."
"Oh no!" cried Mademoiselle. "Don't sell the family jewels."
"There aren't any jewels, my lady," said Lord Yalding.
"Oh yes, there are," said Mabel. "Come and see."
"Let's see what Mabel shows us," said Mademoiselle. "At least it will be amusing."
"It will be amusing," Jimmy promised.
Gerald and Kathleen stayed behind to help Mabel's aunt clean up. So Jimmy and Mabel led the way to the treasure room. Mademoiselle and Lord Yalding followed, holding hands.
"It's much safer to walk hand in hand," Lord Yalding said. "You never know what will happen with these children."
Lord Yalding did not know what to think as he followed the children. They seemed to believe in the magic ring. They also seemed to believe the strange stories they told.
When they reached the treasure room, Mabel said, "Now you'll see."
The others gathered around her.
"There's a secret button here somewhere." Mabel's fingers fumbled for the button.
"Where?" said Lord Yalding.
" Here ," Mabel said impatiently. "Only I can't find it!"
Everyone felt for the button, but no one could find it. The button that revealed the jewels had disappeared.
"I've had enough of this whole silly business," Lord Yalding said impatiently. "Give me the ring. Since you found it in my castle, it's mine. Let's not hear another word about magic."
"Gerald has the ring," Mabel said miserably.
"Well then, go get him," said Lord Yalding.
Mabel and Jimmy went to find Gerald and Kathleen. The four children returned to the treasure room. Then Gerald tried to remove the ring from his finger.
"I can't get it off," he said. "This ring has a mind of its own!"
"I'll get it off," said Lord Yalding. He pulled and pulled. But he couldn't take the ring off Gerald's finger either.
"Soap will make your finger slippery," said Lord Yalding. "The ring will slide right off." But the children knew that soap wouldn't help.
"I don't understand why I can't find the button," said Mabel. She felt for it again as she spoke. And suddenly the jewels appeared!
"Oh my!" exclaimed Lord Yalding. Mademoiselle exclaimed something in French. Both adults stepped forward to admire the jewels.
"But why now?" asked Mabel. "Why not before?"
"It's probably magic," said Kathleen. "Remember Apollo told us that the ring was the heart of the magic?"
Mabel nodded. "Gerald, take away the ring for a second."
Gerald left the room, and the button disappeared. When he returned, the button reappeared.
"I think that button is very cleverly hidden," said Lord Yalding. "And if those jewels are real—"
"Of course they're real!" cried Mabel.
"I'll take the ring now," said Lord Yalding.
After half an hour and lots of soap, the ring was still on Gerald's finger. Then Lord Yalding said something very impatient again. Gerald suddenly became angry.
"Well, I wish it would come off," said Gerald.
Of course the ring came off instantly.
"Thank you," said Lord Yalding. And he put the ring on his own finger.
"He probably thinks it's my fault the ring was stuck," Gerald muttered.
The next morning Lord Yalding came to see Mademoiselle. He went into the sitting room and closed the door. Kathleen and Jimmy stayed away, but Gerald sat on the stairs.
He couldn't hear any of the conversation in the sitting room. But he could see the door. After a while Lord Yalding came out of the sitting room. He looked very gloomy as he put on his straw hat.
The sitting room door was open. Gerald could hear crying. He entered the sitting room and found Mademoiselle sobbing into a couch pillow.
"It's all over," Mademoiselle said. "He won't marry me!" She explained what had happened.

Last night Lord Yalding took a walk around the castle. He was wearing the ring, so he saw the statues move. Then he wished he was a statue. He swam to the island and feasted with the gods. At dawn he wished he was back to normal.
And he decided that he must be mad.
"He told me a madman must not marry," said Mademoiselle.
"Did he talk to the gods?" asked Gerald.
"Yes, and that was the maddest of all his ideas," said Mademoiselle. "Hermes told him to go to some temple tomorrow night. He must go when the moon rises."
"That's right," said Gerald. "We must all go. I can't explain, Mademoiselle. But I give you my word of honor that everything will be all right."
The next night the four children and Mademoiselle walked across the castle lawn. The moon had not yet risen.
They walked until they reached a hilltop where there was a circle of huge stones. One had an odd-looking hole near the top.
"This must be the Temple of Strange Stones," thought Gerald.
Lord Yalding was already sitting there. He told Mademoiselle to leave.
"Never!" she cried, kneeling next to him. "If you are mad, then I am mad too. I believe the children's tales. I'm here to see whatever the rising moon will show us."
Lord Yalding put the ring on her finger, and they stood together.
A faint grayness touched the top of the rock with the hole. Then the hole was a disk of light as a moonbeam shone through it. Suddenly a fountain of light was released.
All sorts of statues—dinosaurs, dragons, angels—began to approach the circle. Last of all came the gods and goddesses from the island.
Each stone statue came quietly into the circle of light. Hermes had told the children to ask about the magic at the Temple of Strange Stones. But no one said a word.
The light started to move away.
"I want to go to the passage on the island," Mademoiselle said suddenly.
The two adults and the children rowed to the island and found the steps.
Guided by candles they walked through the darkness toward the glowing statue of Psyche. They were in the Hall of Granted Wishes.

"I realized something at the Temple of Strange Stones," Mademoiselle explained to Lord Yalding. "The ring is the magic ring given long ago to a mortal. It was given to your ancestor by one of my ancestors. She wanted him to build her a house. So this place was built partly by his love and partly by magic. But she never lived to see it. That was the price of the magic."
"The price?" asked Lord Yalding.
"Whenever you use the ring, it requires a payment," said Mademoiselle. "Your price for wishing for me to appear was to go mad."
"What's our payment?" asked Gerald.
"Children don't have to pay," said Mademoiselle. "For us adults only one wish is free, and that is the last wish. Shall I wish it?"
"Yes!" they all said.
"I wish that all the magic done by this ring will be undone." She turned to Lord Yalding. "And that this ring will be just a charm that binds us together."
The enchanted light surrounding Psyche instantly went out. The scenes of granted wishes went dark. Then Psyche's statue disappeared. In its place was a stone.
"It is my ancestor's grave," said Mademoiselle.

They returned to the castle. The next day Mademoiselle awoke and found a plain gold ring clasped in her hand. More than half the jewels in the treasure room were gone. Large pieces of the castle itself were missing. The children realized that Lord Yalding's ancestor had used the ring to help him build it.

But there were enough jewels left to pay for anything Lord Yalding wanted. And what he wanted was to marry Mademoiselle. By the end of the summer, he had his wish. The ring was slipped onto Mademoiselle's finger and she became Lady Yalding.
They lived happily ever after. And each year during the holidays, their young friends visited them at the castle.
